Between the story, absolute banger of a soundtrack lineup, a UI flashy enough to enjoy just looking at, and a Terminal with basically no learning curve, absolutely phenomenal.

A highly immersive game given how graphically simple it is: basically just a bunch of text and menus. The world-building makes you really feel like a hacker being hired by various people to do all sorts of tasks. I enjoyed the game more than a lot of far more visually impressive games.

I must stress that the 'hacking' part is vastly simplified. It barely touches the basics of hacking, so don't expect the game to teach you how to hack in real-life, though it might just inspire you to learn it properly yourself. The technical aspect of the gameplay also starts to get repetitive once you've tried out all the commands and programs available to you, somewhere around the half-way point. However, the real thrill and challenge of the game lies in digging up useful information and files in the various devices you hack into, analyse them and then figure out how you can use them in order to accomplish your goal. In a sense, this feels like a hacking-themed detective game. There's also a story to the game that really picks up near the end, though some might find it a bit vague at parts.

While I thoroughly enjoyed the game from start to finish, I have to say that this game isn't for everyone. First of all, you gotta be prepared to read a lot. You don't have to read all the text, as many of the text files are purely comedic in nature, having nothing to do with accomplishing the task at hand and are just there to entertain you, but on the other hand, there are a lot of them that contain vital information towards completing your task, even if you don't realise it at first. You definitely need to be patient and observant if you want to beat the game on your own, as well as having good deductive skills to put the information you find to good use. The game does make you think a bit, though not to the extent of typical puzzle games. There are also educational text files that teach you how the various commands and programs in the game work. If you enjoy reading, then I'm sure you would enjoy this game, though there are a few typos here and there that can be annoying.

As for the gameplay, when you're not reading stuff, you're pretty much just typing away commands on your keyboard or just clicking buttons that appear on screen on the UI with your mouse. You don't have to type out everything in full, as you can use the Tab key to auto-complete commands and file names, but it does help to have good typing skills, especially as there are quite a few timed challenges in the game.

All in all, Hacknet does a great job as a hacking simulator game, making you feel like an actual hacker while still being fun to play, even if the hacking aspect is significantly dumbed-down. I recommend this game to those who wish to experience what it's like to be one of those hackers you often see in movies without having to deal with the high technical difficulty of actual hacking. Experienced hackers might find it too simple to be enjoyable, though.

Getting the hang of how the shell command is supposed to be implemented in the game is a little tricky if you've tunneled before because it doesn't work like you'd expect, but everything else is realistic enough to a beginning BASH user that this game is pretty immersive.  I haven't needed to use BASH in a few months, and this ended up being a fun way to dust off several cobwebs.

I'm not entirely sure what the target demographic is for this game. It's an ostensibly terminal-based game running on a UNIX platform, but it has minimal overlap with bash commands, and trying to treat it like bash will only get you confused. 

So, this must be aimed at people without any tech background. However, how much fun can someone uninterested enough in coding to not care about this have, if all they're doing is typing in the same auto-completing commands over and over into a terminal?

Oh, and you can't scroll on the terminal, too. On the other hand, the GUI is both cluttered and unintuitive. Everything feels horrid to use.

It claims to feature "REAL HACKING", but the hacking consists of running magic hack spells via the terminal, and, if you DO know anything about hacking, that makes a lot of what the game asks of you feel obtuse. It took me so long to realise that I was supposed to open up a shell on my own PC, which, if crashed, would somehow take down a proxy server hosted elsewhere? I was assuming I had to find some kind of initial access mechanism to bypass the proxy and execute shellcode on the target PC, but, uh, I guess crashing the equivalent of cmd.exe on my computer really is the future of hacking.

The story is okay, I guess. At least it was easy to 100%.

My advice to anyone interested in a hacking-type game aimed at beginners is to check out the (free!) OverTheWire Bandit wargame, instead; it's fun, and it'll actually teach you something useful.

Hacknet is not the most realistic hacking game, but it's the closest to making you feel like a movie hacker. Know this distinction going in, and you'll likely enjoy yourself.

A new player will likely find that the main story takes 3-5 hours to finish, depending on their familiarity and comfort with using command line interfaces. The DLC, Labyrinths, adds another couple of hours, and is very much worth the small price tag.

The puzzles themselves start very simple, and get more complex over time, with a couple of exceptions - optional "contract" missions that are much more intensive than the rest found at a similar point in time. These harder missions are my favorite part of the game - nothing is impossible, but you actually need to think, take notes, and do (in-game) research. Labyrinths ups the difficulty a little bit, especially towards the end, but seems to be designed for playing before you finish the main game.

Them there are the extensions - user-created campaigns using the same base gameplay mechanics. Some of these are as good as or, arguably, better than the base game, ex. HellSec. With the number of workshop items available, you can easily get 40+ hours out of the game.

For those interested in creating their own extensions, the game comes with a comprehensive tutorial for creating custom content that requires minimal knowledge.

Also of note is the mod system called Pathfinder. I haven't found anything made using it, although I haven't searched super hard, either. It is a modding API and mod loader written in C# available on Nexus. If you're interested in creating your own functionality beyond what extensions can provide, this is your place to look.

Overall, I love this game. It's not realistic, but it's not trying to be.

Overall, Hacknet is a really enjoyable and gripping game with a really unique gameplay style (standing out from the other bs "hacking" simulators) using a lot of fairly realistic set of tools. The story is also really well written and keeps you wanting to complete the next contract, and then the next, so much so that I finished the entire game in a day.

There is no overarching narrative; you're completing puzzles with no purpose. 

Thus, the puzzles are the focus of the game. However, the puzzles are simple and boring. Simple puzzles can still be interesting. Imagine a child's toy where you fit shapes through their respective holes. You can keep yourself busy for a little bit. This game is similar, but everything is a square. How many times can you fit the square in the square hole before it gets boring? Example: you need the password to decrypt a file and you'll find it on the same system within a file called "password.txt". 

Firewall solving requires no input from the player, it's just a timesink. You call the "analyze" command and wait a few seconds at a time until it reveals the answer. You need to call this command multiple times before it starts to reveal the answer - what gameplay function does this serve? Sometimes you don't have any other task to do while the analyze command is processing, so you just wait and wait.. like an idle game. 

Overloading a proxy server involves clicking a button and waiting a few seconds (depending on the number of shells you have up). There's no depth.

Missions share objectives in the form of notes on your computer. For some reason, the devs thought it was a bright idea to have notes take up a significant portion (~30% sometimes) of your memory. So you often have to write up your own abbreviated notes or you won't have enough memory to run the programs you need to crack the ports. The game is fighting itself.

The UI is a mess. A couple hours and your network map becomes an unintelligible mess with no tools to label systems or otherwise organize it. Missions could at least highlight linked servers.

The music is repetitive. Music can make or break a game. In this case, I found myself shutting off music to play my own playlist in the background so I wouldn't be bored to tears while doing all of the waiting the game requires.
